title: Bengaluru Startup Akashalabdhi Flies Inflatable Habitat Structure to 30 km in Balloon Test
excerpt: The 250-litre rigidizable structure deployed, inflated and held its shape at the edge of space in a TIFR balloon flight from Hyderabad — and survived a landing its makers expected to damage it.
body:
• Bengaluru-based Akashalabdhi Space has flown a 250-litre rigidizable inflatable structure to about 30 km aboard a high-altitude balloon from TIFR's National Balloon Facility in Hyderabad.
  • The test checked whether the structure could deploy from a compact package, inflate, and then rigidise — holding its shape without continuous internal pressure.
  • At 30 km the structure faced pressure of just 1–2% of sea level and temperatures near −50°C; it also carried an IISc microbial experiment and a Swiss perovskite solar-cell payload.
  • The module survived landing without the damage the team expected — one of the mission's notable results, its CEO told the Times of India.

A Bengaluru startup building inflatable habitats for space has passed a demanding dress rehearsal in the stratosphere. Akashalabdhi Space flew an experimental 250-litre rigidizable inflatable structure to an altitude of about 30 kilometres aboard a high-altitude balloon early on Tuesday, in a 25 kg mission conducted through the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research's National Balloon Facility in Hyderabad, the Times of India reported.

What the test proved — and what it didn't

The point of the flight was the structure's party trick: it launches folded into a compact package, inflates at altitude, and then rigidises, holding its shape without depending continuously on internal pressure. That is the core technology behind expandable habitats and orbital factories — large working volumes that do not need equally large rockets to carry them. At 30 km, the structure worked through pressure of only 1–2% of sea-level values and temperatures around −45 to −50°C, and the flight also exercised its onboard electronics, power systems, sensors, autonomous controls and telemetry in the cold and near-vacuum. The company is careful about the limits: a balloon flight does not simulate sustained microgravity, orbital vacuum or the full radiation environment of space.

"The module, which was expected to sustain some damage during landing, absorbed the impact without the anticipated damage. The ability of the structure and its protective systems to withstand landing loads is important for future missions involving the recovery of experimental hardware and materials from space."

— Siddarth Jena, CEO, Akashalabdhi Space, to the Times of India

Two passengers with their own agendas

The structure did not fly empty. It carried the Microbial Regolith Experiment from Professor Aloke Kumar's laboratory at the Indian Institute of Science, which studies whether microbial processes can bind regolith — the loose soil covering the Moon and Mars — into construction material, potentially reducing what future lunar missions must haul from Earth. A second payload, an experimental perovskite solar cell from Switzerland-based Perovskia Solar, tested how the technology responds to low pressure, low temperatures and changing sunlight. Kumar said the flight would give his team the data and confidence to prepare for an orbital test. Two results were still being confirmed when the report was filed: the solar cell's performance, and whether the parachute recovery hit its target descent speed of 5 metres per second.

The road to orbit

The flight is part of the company's ANTARIKSHAB programme to develop expandable infrastructure for orbital manufacturing and habitation. Akashalabdhi, incubated at IISc, earlier completed ground qualification tests in Switzerland — pressure and leak-before-burst tests, thermal cycling, ageing and impact tests simulating micrometeoroid strikes — aimed at Technology Readiness Level 6. In January, the company outlined plans for a scaled orbital habitat of about 70 cubic metres, with a final habitat of around 300 cubic metres. "We position ourselves as a space real estate and infrastructure company," founder-CEO Siddharth Jena told The Hindu BusinessLine. Tuesday's flight is the first time its structure has proven itself at the edge of space rather than in a test chamber.
